en: I also pay homage to the pervasive, manifest [Buddha], who shines like the moon of the *dharmakāya* in the lake of the pure mind, liberated from the Rāhu of the aggregates (*skandha*). Bow down to the orb of the body of enjoyment (*sāmbhogikakāya*), which is the sun of the *dharmakāya*.

I bow to that emanation-body (nairmāṇika-kāya), which is rich with various abodes of transformation, to be realized for the sake of accomplishment by the great seers; which, like a wish-fulfilling tree, grants the requests of the world when it is not yet a wish-fulfiller; and which is visible only to those of meritorious deeds.
I bow to the Sage’s True Dharma, which is peaceful, supreme among those things free from passion, and the exclusive domain of yogins; it is ungraspable and ineffable,
following the individual wisdom of those who have entered the various stages according to reality.
I bow to the Dharma taught for the enjoyment [of the Buddhas], which is to be grasped through meditative concentration.
May the command of the Buddha—which conforms to the various languages of gods, demons, and others;
which has transcended its own [conventional] characteristics; and which is as clear as crystal—purify you!
In accordance with the various dispositions of those to be trained, they appear in forms such as Brahmā and others;
established on the stages beginning with the "imageless," those Bodhisattvas are victorious.
Having perceived the world as mind-only, like a dream, they strive for the welfare of beings.
I praise those who have entered the seven stages beginning with *muditā*.
I worship those who, seeing the world afflicted by suffering like a mother [sees her child], and being themselves pained by that suffering,
bind the jewel of their minds to awakening (*bodhi*) for the sake of its liberation.

King Śrī Jayavarman was the possessor of the kingdom of Vyomadvārāṅga, his lotus-feet being licked by the swarms of bees that were the crowns of bowing kings. Even though the sun is impartial, it rises as a benefactor for him.
He was the immediate upraising of the virtuous and the spontaneous destruction of the darkness of the wicked.
Like a father, he bore his subjects along the path to heaven and liberation;
with the rays of his memory, he restrained the horses of his senses from wandering onto wrong paths.
In the path of the righteous, in accordance with the legal tradition of Manu and others,
which was obstructed by the darkness of time, he appeared like the midday sun;
in him, virtues such as heroism were established as his very essence.

By that splendor, he was like iron heated in a supreme fire. (14cd) Even though others were restrained with great effort from abducting the wives of others, by him [Śukra], through whatever means possible, the supreme knowledge was himself taken away upon merely hearing it. (15)
He who, with the hands of the Śruti and Smṛti, shall rescue the lady Satyavatī— who had been abandoned by the son of Dharma into the great ocean of the defects of the Kali age;
and upon whom, though she was common to all, rested the science of statecraft among kings.
Like a stream of rain from the clouds, he was a purifier for those yet to come, serving as a sanctuary of sacred sites (tīrtha) for all beings.
Like a father, he acted as a beloved protector for his subjects who were oppressed,
wiping away their tears with his spies who resembled outstretched hands.
Attending upon him was the learned Ācārya Kīrti-paṇḍita, who had crossed to the further shore of the ocean of knowledge; he was like the full moon of widespread fame,
having traversed the oceans of all the scriptures by means of the boat of his own prowess.
Having obtained the jewels of the true meaning of reality, he distributed them among those who sought the wealth of wisdom.
His virtues, such as benevolence and the like, were renowned by nature, like the heat of fire;
whereas his faults were merely adventitious, like the malleability of iron.
If anger and other such passions ever manifested within his heart in any way,
they quickly came under the control of his knowledge, like playful serpents.
Day after day, at the four junctions of the day, he remained absorbed in yoga and was endowed with the four kinds of generosity.
He who taught the Dharma consisting of the four seals to the fourfold assembly;
he who, though having acquired immeasurable wealth for the sake of renunciation, was rich in the treasure of wisdom;
and he who was proclaimed by the learned as being enriched by the meaning of the six baskets.
He who was the agent of the *parasmaipada* in all actions toward all beings,
yet never at any time employed the *ātmanepada* as instructed by anyone—
having vanished like the onset of darkness during the rainy season for the worlds.
When that [teaching] had proceeded, the moon of the Buddha’s Dharma shone forth in the purity of autumn;
the sun of the vision of selflessness, mind-only, and so forth, having dispelled the night of false views, shone once more like day. (26cd–27)
He who rekindled the lamp of the path of the True Dharma— the treatise beginning with the *Madhyavibhāga*—
which had been extinguished by the winds of the faults of the age;
he who, having sought out one of profound wisdom, brought back from a foreign land a text of one hundred thousand verses.
While this man was teaching the *Tattvasaṃgraha-ṭīkā* and other tantras,
those arrogant elephants among logicians, who had taken refuge at the side of kings,
became devoid of pride upon encountering the son of Śākyasiṃha, appearing like the minions of Yama.
Even the mere mention of his disciple’s name, falling upon the ears of disputants,
produced terror like a mantra within a circle of snakes.
He was honored as a preceptor by kings together with their delighted harems.

Seated upon the Dharma-throne, he repeatedly taught the Buddha-dharma. His speech, which constantly brought glory to the kings of Kambuja, consisted of the realization of place, time, and self, as well as the examination of the marks of others.

... having propitiated the king with efforts imbued with conciliation, he released even those deserving of death out of fear of various kings. Seeing that ascetics had met with calamity while performing the king's service, [he rescued them]. 34ab–35ab.
He by whom they were reported to the king and released, and who was established in the right course;

he whom the king, having honored him, appointed for the protection of the kingdom and its territories, and who was constantly employed within the palace for rites of pacification, nourishment, and so forth. (35cd–36)

He restored the Sage, whose body had been fashioned from compassion, who had been established for the sake of protecting the Buddhist faith during times of calamity, and whose seat had once again been broken;
he did so while entreating him to lead all the worlds through the gateway of liberation.
He who joyfully offered to the Sage a gateway adorned with gold and silver,
thereby securing for others the non-dual, unsurpassed vehicle as if it were his own;
he who presented to the Sage two palanquins, one of gold and one of silver.
He constructed for the sage a great copper-roofed palace, rich with jewels and gold, containing a celestial lion-throne; he who,
seeking the fruit of acting for the sake of another, built this on that most excellent field where the sage resided.
He assigned four thousand khārīs of grain to the sage. Having established the outer and inner true Dharma, he constructed separate hermitages for the sake of honoring that Saṅgha and for guests.
He gave many lordly elephants, female elephants, horses, buffaloes, bulls, cows,
hermitages, enjoyments, and male and female slaves to the sage;
these were established in that place for the stability of the sun of the entire lineage of the learned.

By Śrī Satyavarman, who re-established the broken seats of the ten additional images of Vajrin and Lokeśvara on Mount Prāggu, was established the Prajñāpāramitā, the savior and mother of the Protectors. (44cd–45)
He established images of the World-Protectors and others in Tuṅgādri, his own renowned city, as well as in Kumārāmbhapura; and he restored numerous ancient,
perfected Buddha-images throughout the various directions that had previously been broken.

He further restored the hermitages and reservoirs; even the circle of that Sage’s disciples, who were favorably disposed toward men, constructed many such monuments for the Muni, complete with palaces and endowed with all prosperity. 48ab–48cd.
...in the village of Dharmapaṭṭana, for the sake of accomplishing the welfare of himself and others, he established [the images] in the Śaka year six hundred and nine (609).
All of this was done by him solely by the command of the king. 49–50ab.
... by the power of the fire of the *piṇḍa*...
|| 50cd This is the command of the illustrious Jayavarman, which follows the Buddha's Dharma;
it should be emulated by the Buddhists for the sake of attaining liberation and worldly prosperity. || 51ab–51cd

Those groups of constellations that are remembered as headed by Pūrvaphalgunī are considered the most excellent; they are regarded as the lords of the twelve months. Possessing great heroism and great supernatural power, they cause the waning and waxing [of time] in the world.
They behold all creatures devoted to both dharma and adharma;
then, through uneven rains and winds, they strike down the most wicked.
These gods and nāgas, being impartial, bring delight to those who are most righteous.

Therefore, for the sake of sentient beings, the twelve festivals as described by the Teacher should be performed month by month in their proper sequence by one who desires happiness. O Great Sage, [the images] installed in the direction of Agni should be brought back to their original positions.
Every day, at the three times of day, the self-controlled one should worship and strike the Gāṇḍīva bow.
Because its purifying sound signals the time for the community's duties, those who hear it even with their mind alone are blessed; they have gone to the third heaven.

He who, having caused a monastery to be built, dedicates it to the Three Jewels for the sake of accomplishing the welfare of others, shall obtain great merit. One-third of all enjoyments is dedicated to the Triple Gem.
It should be established separately so that it does not become mixed with others.
If the formal authorization (*jñapti*) for the monastery has not been performed by the monks according to the rule, it should be known as a non-monastery; indeed, it is merely a storehouse.
This which has been done for the sake of livelihood is neither for the sake of others nor for peace;
there is no merit of the Brahman therein by which one might attain omniscience.
When the formal authorization for a monastery has been performed according to the proper rule, [then it is meritorious].
Therefore, merit is like the sky—pervading everywhere and inexhaustible. 62cd Thus, those lowest of men who destroy such merit experience terrible and endless suffering in hell. 63ab–63cd
Householders must not consume anything that exceeds the share of the Saṅgha’s property;
for while mantras and other means can counteract poison, they cannot [counteract] what belongs to the Saṅgha.
Having thus kept these words of the Omniscient One in mind with devotion, [one should act accordingly]. 64ab–65ab.
The learned one, having properly established the monastery, remained at a distance.
Those who were virtuous, possessed of good conduct, and wise were appointed as the superintendents of the community. Various enjoyments were provided for their sake by him who desired merit.
Whatever ritual action for self-restrained ascetics has been prescribed by the Sage at dawn and other times—
all that must be performed by the community, and especially by the officiating priest.
At all sacrifices, the members of the community must not go unless they have been invited.
Even if they have come of their own accord for one's benefit, these [others] share in the sin there.
One who is skilled in the heart-seals, mantras, and vidyās, in the rite of fire-offerings (homa),
and who knows the secret of the vajra and bell, is a worthy recipient of offerings and a domestic priest.

On the auspicious festival days, the domestic priest should perform the bathing and other rites for the sage with the chanting of Vedic hymns, Ṛṣisūkta, and Brahmaghoṣa, accompanied by the consecration of water.
Through such enlightened bathing and ceremonies, people become happy and their righteousness increases.
For all beings, both moving and unmoving, are indeed contained within the body of the Omniscient One.
Dependent origination is the Brahma-voice; the True Dharma is the Bull’s roar. It is well-spoken and the definitive realization of peace; it is remembered as the Veda of Verses (Gāthā-veda).

When the sciences such as *brahmaghoṣa* and others are recited upon my head, then that head is most auspicious; such is the teaching of the Omniscient One. Furthermore, during the consumption [of food], in the mouth, at the transition [of breath], or when any portent has arisen—
The bathing and other rites for the Teacher should be performed so that peace may prevail among the people.
(74cd) With faith, for the strengthening of men and for the increase of the teaching, the wise man should perform the instruction of the Dharma on every auspicious day. (75ab–75cd)
... or according to one's strength; 76ab ... by those who have reached the ultimate refuge; 76cd ...
rendered into a state of non-existence; 77ab.
Having established devotion with his mind, he bowed with palms joined in *añjali*;
even though other [deities] were present, he should offer the oblation to Śarva. 77cd–78ab/78cd.

...the six alone are desired as the primary means for accomplishing Dharma. (79ab) ...Dharma always increases everywhere through that [practice]. (79cd) ...slightly moving his face while concentrating his mind on a single object. (80ab)
... even by merely saying "I am," one would obtain infinite merit.
(80cd) If all sentient beings were to perform every kind of meritorious deed, the Sage has declared that the merit of a single upholder of the True Dharma is greater than that. (81)
Therefore, the wise person who has abandoned other duties and dwells in the monastery always embraces the true Dharma through writing and other such means,
being adorned with correct conduct and appointed to the affairs of the monastery.
All teachers who have appeared should be honored according to one's ability.
(83cd) Gracious speech preceded by proper conduct, as well as grass, water, and ground—these are available everywhere and at all times to the virtuous who seek the essence of the body. (84)
For the body is indeed like excrement, a constant abode of all impurities;
nevertheless, it possesses an essence: Dharma is considered to be like a wish-fulfilling tree (kalpavṛkṣa).
Just as from a house being consumed by fire, or from a sinking boat in the ocean... [85–86ab]

The wise should quickly grasp the treasury of Dharma before the perishable body [vanishes]. Seeing that life is unstable, like the flickering glow of a small lamp tossed by the force of the wind, the learned man does not commit what ought not to be done.
Even an insentient woman, about to enter the fire, regards death with equanimity;
what need has she for all her worldly possessions? How much more so for those who possess discernment!
He who does not exert effort even toward his own welfare in this world should not exert effort for the sake of heaven or liberation.
He is like a chisel for the purpose of cutting down the tree of his mother's youth;
even a wicked person who lives for an eon brings about intense suffering. Indeed, a long life is accumulated only to the great misfortune of living beings.
Any worship of the Blessed One devised by sacrificial priests, teachers, and others,
should be nurtured with efforts preceded by faith, like one's own mother.
A sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) must be given to the officiating priests and others every year.
One should provide daily food along with clothing for the monks who preach the Dharma.
Even when the property of the Saṅgha is exhausted,
he who sells jewels for the sake of worshipping the Saṅgha shares in that merit, even if the jewels belong to the Protector himself.
Those authorized over the monastery and others should expand that site;
they must especially not destroy it, for that would lead to the commission of great sin.
Having reached a holy abode, a sinner is purified through remorse.
But having destroyed that [attachment] while remaining therein, for the sake of purification, where will he go?

(95cd) Gardens, fields, slaves, and so forth, dedicated to the Three Jewels, are not under one's control regarding kinsmen, as they are subject to the local authorities, the grain-officials, and other masters. (96ab–96cd)

From the outer gate until they reach the interior, men—even if they are offenders—must not be struck with even a whip or addressed with harsh words. This is the command of the wise; this is the path for achieving memory, intelligence, and other such qualities.
Like the tongue of an elixir that destroys all defects,
the *aparavaktra* meter alone should be employed here by the wise for the attainment of their purpose; for some have indeed said this,
though it was previously stated by the Omniscient One that the path to liberation is different from the path to heaven, which is the subject of this royal discourse.
Even a sinner who follows this command would transform the poison of his evil into nectar;
whereas one of virtuous deeds who transgresses it would turn the nectar of his merit into poison.
